about: The words of the chain riddle_trail (Data/encounters/chain_riddle_trail_793.json; Design/content/chains/riddle_trail.md): the rune sticks that lead from Dorestad to Salhaugar by the Danish kings' hall. Every title, intention, line and label key of its thirteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the one news item the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. No riddle's answer is given away in a line, a label or an outcome: the answers are the chest's to keep. People: Ravn (the hand), Beornwine (the lookout) and Aldger (the steersman) are the spine's cast; Hroald and Gunnvald are the two names on the Snoldelev stone (DR 248) and everything said of them beyond those names is invented; the skipper, the carter, the ship's master, the ferryman, the steward, the swineherd, the skald and the carver are ordinary invented people without names. Nothing is quoted: the riddles are told by their images in our own words, the last question likewise, and Alcuin's line about Ingeld is our own plain rendering of his Latin. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A stick from a guest

A Danish skipper in from Ripa walks the dam asking which boat is the Frisian's with the Northman in it. When he finds yours he holds out a stick of ash wood, a hand long, squared, and cut with runes on all four sides.
I was asked to put this in your hand. Not your man's hand. Yours. I was told to say that twice.
Who sent it? A guest. That is the name he gave, and at my age I do not ask a man for a second one.
When you know what it means, say it to the carter at the landing at Ripa. The one with the two red oxen. He will know if you are right. He knows very little else.
Old cutting. Look at that sign, the one like a gate with a bar across. Nobody under fifty cuts it so. It says a man went out from home and saw a way of ways.
You had the first one from me, and you got it. This is the second, and it is not from me. Somebody has been counting.
Take the stick and put it in the chest
Have Ravn read it to you, sign by sign
Say a Frisian carries cloth, not kindling
The stick goes into the chest with the tally sticks, and looks much like them. The Dane nods and goes back to his hides. Ravn watches him all the way down the dam.

Ravn reads it with his thumb, one sign at a time, and makes you say each sound after him. It takes until the tide turns. You know six runes now and one riddle. He does not tell you the answer and he does not say whose hand cut it.
The Dane shrugs and lays the stick on your thwart anyway. "Then burn it," he says, "and say at Ripa that you were cold." It is still there in the morning. Nobody aboard has burnt it.
The carter at the landing

At the landing at Ripa a carter stands by two red oxen with nothing in his cart. He looks at the stick in your belt before he looks at your cargo, and then he looks at the sky, like a man who has been told not to speak first.
Three Frisian boats since the spring and none of them had a stick. I had begun to think he had sent it by a fool.
This is how it goes. You say the answer. If it is right I give you what he left and the next stick. If it is wrong I still give you the next stick, but I am allowed to laugh.
You have the look of a man who knows. Go on. I drive over one twice a day, so do not try to tell me it is something else.
You have the look of a man who has carried a thing a long way without opening it. Well. That is my trade too.
Give him the answer
Buy the ale and let him say it himself (4 d)
Say you do not know, and help him load instead

He slaps the near ox for joy. Out of his shirt come a twist of silver wire, weighed against your own pennies at twenty, and a second stick, shorter, about a beast with too many legs. "And sell your cloth here, not further north. They are short of it till the moon turns."

He drinks your ale and says the answer with his mouth full of bread, so that you are not sure of it even now. Then he gives you the second stick. "He did not say you had to be clever. Only that you had to come."

He laughs, as he was allowed to. You load his cart with another man's hides for an hour. At the end of it he puts the second stick in your hand. "A man who will carry what he does not understand. He will like that, or he will not. I never knew which."
A hail across the water
A Norse ship alters course to pass close under your lee. Her master stands on the stern with one hand on the stay and a stick in the other, and shouts a question over the water.
Frisian! I nearly ran you under. I have been looking for you in this since the morning, which is a joke, and you will see why when you read the stick.
Frisian! One small boat, four men, a Northman at the sheet. He said I could not miss you. He was wrong by nine days.
The carter's one first. Four that walk and four that hang. Shout it, and shout it right, and I will throw you something that shines.
I am for the Slie. The ferryman there has the next, and he is slower than I am. Take wine if you have it. They are drinking water and calling it a virtue.
Shout the carter's answer across
Close with him and take the stick by hand
Hold your course; a strange ship is a strange ship

He roars it back to his own crew, who cheer as if they had bet on it. A ring of silver wire comes over the water and Ravn takes it out of the air. The stick follows, tied to a net float. It is about a huge thing that fears nothing but the wind.

The two hulls touch and part. He hands the stick down himself. "You did not answer. I do not blame you. I shouted mine wrong at the first man too." His ship is a spot on the sea before you have the sail drawing again.

You hold your course. He passes a boat's length off, laughing, and throws the stick. It lands in the bilge. "Careful is good," he shouts. "The old man was never careful and look at him now." He does not say what there is to look at.
The ferry on the Slie

The ferryman on the Slie pushes your pennies back across the thwart. He wants a word from you instead, and under his seat, tied to the rib with tarred cord, there is a small bag that hangs as silver hangs.
No fare. I have been paid for you already, and overpaid. Sit. The crossing is as long as I choose to make it.
You have met a carter, a shipman and me. Did you not wonder? We all sat on one bench when we had hair. The low bench, by the door, in a hall you will see soon enough.
He calls himself Gest on the sticks. A guest. It is not his name. His name you can earn. He taught the four of us to hold a hundred verses in our heads, and we have each kept about six.
There are more spears than merchants on this shore since King Godfred came with his ships. I row them over all the same. A spearman's backside is as heavy as a trader's and pays worse.

After me it is Zealand. Go up the long fjord to Hleidr and ask for the man who cannot count the king's swine. Do not ask at the hall. They will send you to the skald, and the skald will send you home.
Tell him what swallows water and woods and fears the wind
Take the other oar for a day and listen
Pay him to say plainly where the sticks come from (10 d)

He ships his oars in the middle of the water and cuts the bag loose. Ring silver, hacked small: it weighs out at a hundred and twenty pennies. "He said the one who got this far was to be paid as a man is paid, not as a boy." The next stick is about brides in white hoods. He talks Danish at you the whole way back and by the far bank you are following half of it.

You row. He talks. Eleven crossings, a horse that will not board, two fights about the fare. By evening you have a blistered hand, a share of the day's takings and more Danish than you came with. He gives you the stick about the white-hooded brides. The bag stays under his seat. "That was for the answer. This was for the back."

He takes your ten pennies and weighs them, since he does not trust a king's face on silver. "From Hleidr. From an old man by the mounds. There. You have bought with money what the others earned, and it is worth what money is worth." He gives you the stick all the same.
The hand at the cutting

On the night watch Ravn lays the four sticks side by side on the thwart and runs his thumb along the cuts, as a man feels a blade he once owned. He has known whose hand it is since Dorestad. Tonight he looks as if he might say so.
This sign. The gate with the bar. I cut it so myself, because the man who taught me cut it so, and I was beaten when I did not.
Hroald. He sat at the king's feet at Hleidr and held the old words: who begot whom, which verse goes after which, what was sworn and by whom. Not a skald. A skald makes. Hroald kept.
We had that word at Gyrwe. Thyle. In the old songs he is the man who sits at the king's feet and remembers what everyone else in the hall would rather forget.
I was the best he had. He said so once, to someone else. Then one Yule he asked me a thing before the whole hall, and I answered it. That was the mistake. Not the answer I gave. That I gave one.
Ask him what the last question was
Take his watch at the oar and let him talk or not
Tell him a hand does not keep a secret from the man who pays him

He cuts it for you on the back of a tally stick by the light of the lamp, and reads it out once. It is about what a father said in his dead son's ear. "I said something clever. The hall laughed. Hroald did not. I took ship in the spring and I have not been up that fjord since."

You take the oar. For a long while there is only the water. Then he tells it, all of it, to the sea rather than to you: the bench, the Yule, the question about the father and the dead son, the laughter. Before light he cuts the question on a stick and puts it in your chest himself. "So that there are two of us who cannot answer it."

He looks at you for the time it takes a wave to pass under the boat. "Hroald. Salhaugar, by Hleidr. There is your wage's worth." He gathers the sticks, gives them back to you, and takes the bow watch though it is not his turn. The rest he keeps.
Where the king's swine root
Below the great hall at Hleidr the steward bars the path with his staff. Behind him a swineherd is counting pigs out of a pen, aloud, and does not get the same number twice.
A Frisian with cloth is welcome at the landing. A Frisian with sticks wants something at the hall, and at the hall I am the door.
The ferryman's one, then. The brides who walk the reefs. Old Hroald said that whoever came would know it, and that if he did not know it I was to feed him and send him down the fjord again.
Ten tongues. No. Twenty eyes, that is right, I counted the eyes. It walks, the old man says, and I am to ask what it is. I have it in the pen and I still do not know.
The king drinks here in three nights. Strangers sit by the door and are asked things. If you want the old man, that is the road to him. He does not see anybody the hall has not laughed at first.
Name the white-hooded brides for the steward
Help drive the pigs to the oak wood, and hear his riddle on the way
Give the steward a guest's gift (20 d)

The steward lifts his staff. "By the door, in three nights. Bring your own knife." The swineherd gives you his riddle in a rush, wrong the first time. And a boy brings a broken stick from the midden behind the hall, with the first words gone. "The old man threw that one away himself," the steward says. "So it is likely the best."

Two days in the oak wood behind the king's pigs. Aldger says nothing about it, loudly. The swineherd tells you his riddle nine times, and on the way home he speaks to the steward, who looks at the mud on you and finds a place for you at the feast after all. It is five nights off now, not three.

The steward turns your gift over, finds nothing wrong with it, and is a little disappointed. "By the door, in three nights. I have let in worse for less." The swineherd shouts his riddle after you down the path.
The low bench

You are seated on the low bench by the door, far from the fire, where the draught is. The king is a shape beyond the smoke with gold on his arm. His skald walks the length of the hall with a full horn in his hand and stops in front of you.
This is the bench. Every man the old one taught sat here first. Mind the third plank. It has been loose since my father's day.
A guest from the south, with a chest full of old Hroald's kindling. Then tell the hall what the swineherd has in his pen: ten tongues, twenty eyes, forty feet, and it walks.
He is not here. He does not come since his son died. He kept what other men made, and called it a craft. I make new, and the king pays me for it, and I am told that is the lesser thing.
King Sigfred likes an answer given quickly. He has waited on Franks at their assemblies and says he is done waiting.
King Godfred is listening. He likes to know what a Frank's merchants are made of before he meets the Frank.
The rule of the bench is older than I am. Answer, and something comes down the hall to you. Fail, and this horn does, and you see the bottom of it before you sit.
Answer the swineherd's riddle before the whole bench
Say you cannot, and drink the horn dry for it
Buy the skald's own riddle of him, and ask where the old man sits (12 d)

You say it. There is a silence the length of a breath, then the benches beat the boards. Something bright passes from hand to hand down the hall: an arm-ring off the king's own arm, a hundred and fifty pennies by weight. The skald sets you one of his own to take away, two meanings in every word, and says quietly: "South-east, a morning's walk. The farm by the mounds. Go in two days. He sleeps after a feast he was not at."

The horn holds more than it looks. You see the bottom of it, and then the roof, and then the faces of your crew. The hall likes a man who pays what he owes. The skald, in a good humour, sets you a riddle of his own for the road and tells you where the old man lives. You will remember that part tomorrow, when Ravn tells it to you again.

He takes your silver across the palm of his hand, as he would from any buyer. The riddle he sells has two meanings in every word. "Hroald is at Salhaugar, a morning's walk to the south-east. Tell him his sticks reached the hall. Tell him the hall had other things to talk about."
Salhaugar

At the farm by the mounds an old man sits on a bench in the sun with his face turned a little to the wrong side of you. His eyes are white. A grey stone as long as a man lies by the door, and nothing is cut on it.
A Frisian. I could smell the tar and the cheese from the gate. Sit. I am Hroald. I was the mouth of this hall for forty winters, and now I am an old man who sends sticks to strangers.

Gunnvald had the seat after me. My son. He held everything I gave him and never once got the order wrong. He died at the winter nights with a cough, in bed, like a farmer. That stone is his. I cannot see to have it cut.

What I know is in one place, and the place is seventy years old and coughs too. So I cut riddles and sent them out by men who owed me, to see who would carry a thing from port to port for no pay he could name. A head like that holds. I hoped for a Dane. One takes what washes up.
And he is with you. I know that step. He put his feet down just so thirty winters ago, walking out of the hall. Stand where you are, boy. I am not done with the Frisian.
A man with no stone is gone when the last one who knew him is gone. He wants the name set up. That much any crew with rollers could do for him.
Master, he has it all by heart and nowhere else. At Gyrwe we would call that a library with one candle in it. Calfskin, scraped. I could write it as he says it. I could try.

I can pay. Gunnvald had rings from two kings. He is lying with the best of them, in the new mound, and the rest are in the house. I tell you so you know I am not a beggar. I am told I should not tell people.
Offer your crew and your rollers to set up the son's stone
Say there is a head in your boat that already holds half of it
Say what is cut in stone lasts, and so does what is written on skin (40 d for calfskins)
Say little, and mark which mound is the new one

"So. Not a head. A back." He is quiet, and then he laughs, the first time. "I asked the sea for a pupil and it sent a carter. Good. There is a man at the hall who cuts. Come again when the moon has been full twice, and bring your rollers."

He turns his white eyes to where Ravn stands. Nobody speaks. "He answered what should not be answered." "He has had thirty winters to think about it," you say. The old man breathes out. "Then let him winter here or come back to it. After Yule, when the days turn, I will ask it once more before the hall. Once." Ravn has not moved. He looks like a man who has been handed something hot.

"Words on a dead calf." He spits. "They will lie there and not say themselves. Nobody will know how the voice goes." Then his hand finds the uncut stone by the door, and stays on it. "But I am having a name cut in a rock so that it lasts. So I am a fool either way. Buy your skins. Have them scraped over the winter. Come when the ice is off the fjord and bring the boy who scratches."

You say what a guest says, and little of it. On the way out you count the mounds. Five old, grown over with thorn. One new, on the south side, where the turf has not knitted. Ravn sees you counting. He does not speak on the walk back, and he is not a man who needs a reason for that, but tonight he has one.
The new mound
No moon. The new mound is the one on the south side, where the turf has not knitted. There are two wooden spades in the boat for digging ballast, and so far the farm's dogs are quiet.

I will say it once. He will know by the morning: a blind man hears his own ground. And every Dane from here to the Slie will know by the autumn. They will not come for you with spears. They will only stop seeing your boat.
Heathen or not, he is a dead man in his grave and we are four men with spades. I have robbed nobody yet, living or otherwise. I would have liked to die able to say so.
I will not carry one. I will not stop you. Those are the two things I can do, and I am doing both.
Dig, quickly, and be down the fjord before light
Pour the ale you brought onto the mound instead, and go
Put the spades back under the thwart and say it was a walk

The turf lifts like a lid. Charred wood, a clay pot, and beside it, not burnt, what the father could not bring himself to put on the fire: rings, twisted and plain, and one broad arm-ring cut with a row of small horns. It weighs out later at eleven hundred pennies and more. You are down the fjord before the cocks. Nobody aboard says a word until the open sea, and then it is only the course.

The dogs. Then torches, and housemen with staves who know their business. When it is over you are on your knees in the yard and the old man is standing over you in his shirt. "I counted your steps going out, Frisian. You counted my mounds." He takes forty pennies for his men's trouble. "And you will haul my son's stone. With that back. Come when the moon has been full twice. You will come." You will.

You pour the ale out on the raw turf, all of it. Aldger looks away and crosses himself. Ravn says something short in his own tongue. Then you go back to the boat. In the morning Ravn says, to nobody: "He needs men with rollers for that stone." It is settled as easily as that.

"It was a walk," you say. "A long one, for a man carrying spades," says Aldger. The spades go back under the thwart. In the morning you send word to the farm that a crew with rollers is at the old man's service for his stone.
Gunnvald's stone

The carver has done. Two rows of runes down the face; above them three horns locked into one another, and a wheel-cross with four bent arms. The stone lies on your rollers at the foot of the mounds, and a hole has been dug for it.
I will read it as it stands, so no man says later it reads otherwise. Gunnvald's stone, Hroald's son's, thul at Salhaugar. I was not told to cut more. I asked.
Put my hand on it. Yes. The gate with the bar across. He has cut it the old way. I told him to. Let them wonder at it when I am gone.
You came. A man who has been in my son's mound to his elbows and still comes back when he is bid. I do not know what you are, Frisian. But you are not a liar. Lift.
That is all of it. His name, mine, the seat, the place. What we held between us is not on it. A stone is not big enough, and no one left has the head for it. So. A name. It is more than most get.
It will stand when the hall has fallen in. Somebody will stop at it and say the name aloud, not knowing who he was. That is the use of it. It is not nothing.
Raise it with your own crew, and stand while he says the name
Pay the carver yourself, so the old man keeps his son's rings (60 d)
Set it upright, take what is owed and catch the tide

Four men, six rollers, a rope and a morning. It stands. The old man says the name three times, to the south, the west and the north, and then stops, as if the east were someone else's business. He pays in his son's rings, eight hundred pennies by weight, and the steward comes down from the hall to say there is a place for the Frisian under the king's hand whenever he lies at Hleidr. At the gate the old man puts a short stick in your hand. It is not a riddle. It says that cattle die and kinsmen die, and one thing does not.

You pay the carver before the old man can reach for his bag. He stands a while with his mouth working. Then it stands, and he says the name. By evening the hall has heard that a Frisian paid for a Dane's stone, and seven hundred pennies of ring silver come down from the king with the steward and a place under the king's hand. The old man gives you one of the three horns that hung over his seat, silver at the lip. "There are three on the stone," he says. "Now you know where one of them went." And a stick, which is not a riddle: cattle die, kinsmen die, and one thing does not.

It stands. You have a tide. The old man weighs out six hundred pennies of rings without a word more than the weight, and the steward names you a guest of the hall, since that was promised. From the fjord you can see the stone for a long time, grey against the green, with a small bent figure in front of it, talking.
The last question

The hall is full and for once it is quiet. The old man has been led to the middle of the floor, between the fires. He turns his white eyes toward your bench, the low one by the door, and asks what he asked Ravn thirty winters ago.
I ask it once. What did the One-eyed say in his son's ear, before the boy was carried to the fire?
I have a ring on the Northman answering. He answered last time. A man does not change what he is because he has been to sea.
Do not help me. Whatever you see me do, do not help me.
Say nothing. It is Ravn's question
Stand up and say it yourself: no man alive knows that
Whisper Ravn a clever answer to give

Ravn stands. He takes a long time. "No man knows that," he says, "and I did not know it then either." The old man lets out a breath he has held for thirty winters. "There. That is the whole of the craft. To know which things you hold and which you do not, and never to fill the gap with your own noise." The king sends rings down the hall and the old man adds his son's: fourteen hundred pennies by weight. A horn from over the high seat. A place for you under the king's hand. The steward's own son to show you the marks of the fjord. Ravn will sail with you while the old man lives. After that, he says, there is a seat he has to go and sit in.

You stand and say it: no man alive knows that. It is right, and the hall beats the boards, and it was not yours to say. The old man turns his face from you to the place beside you. "The Frisian has a head. But I did not ask the Frisian." Ravn says it then, quietly, after you. It is enough. Twelve hundred pennies in rings, a horn, a guest's place. Ravn does not speak to you until the boat is past the narrows. Then he says: "You meant it well," which from him is a hard word.

You whisper him something neat. He does not turn his head. "No man knows that," he tells the hall. Then, louder: "My master here has a guess, if anyone wants it." The hall laughs at the Frisian until the dogs bark. The old man laughs longest. "Thirty winters ago that was you, boy." Six hundred pennies of rings come down the bench for the man who brought him home, and a guest's place, and the skald pays his lost bet with a good grace, to Ravn.
The calfskin book

Nine days of it. The old man speaks with his eyes shut. Beornwine writes with his tongue between his teeth, and Ravn says each line again slowly, so the boy can hear where one word ends. Now there are five gatherings of calfskin, sewn with flax, and the question of where they go.
Read me one back. Any one. No. That is the words. It is not how it goes. Well. A stone does not say how my son laughed, either.

There is no letter for half his sounds. I have used the thorn, and the rune for w, as we do at home, and made up the rest. Any brother who can read English could sound it out. He would not understand a word, but he could sound it.
Master Alcuin wrote to a bishop that a churchman's table wants a reader and not a harper. What has Ingeld to do with Christ, he asked. Master, Ingeld is on the third skin. All of him.
I said it could not be done. It is done badly, which is a different thing. I held all of that once and lost most of it. It will not get lost out of there unless there are mice.
It is your calf, Frisian, and your boy's scratching. Mine was only the breath. So where does it go? Say, and I will tell you if I like it. I will not stop you either way.
Keep the book in your own chest, for the house
Promise it to the school at Eoforwic, which pays for wonders
Leave it at Salhaugar with his daughter's sons, who cannot read it

"A merchant's chest. Between the tally sticks and the scales." He thinks about it. "It has been in worse company. It was in me." He pays for the skins and the nine days in his son's rings, seven hundred pennies by weight, and will not be argued with. The book goes to the bottom of the chest, wrapped in a sealskin. Beornwine reads from it on calm nights, and Ravn tells him where he has it wrong. An heir of yours will open it some day and wonder what house he was born into.

"To the shaven men. Who will keep it in a box and be ashamed of it." He laughs, not kindly. "But they do keep things. I am told they have kept an old king of the south and his songs for longer than there have been Danes." With his rings, and what the masters of the school at Eoforwic give for a thing no library has, it comes to fifteen hundred pennies, and a clerk of the minster who will look after your goods on the Ouse. Beornwine is as happy as you have seen him. Somewhere in that school a man is reading the third skin with his lips moving, and has started to wonder who brought it.

You put it in his hands. He weighs it as he would a child. "My daughter's boys cannot read it. Nor can any man among the Danes." "Somebody will, some day," Beornwine says. "Then let it be here when he comes." It goes into the chest by the old man's bed, under his son's cloak. He gives six hundred pennies of rings and sends to the hall, and the hall names you its guest. On the path Ravn says, "That was the right place," and then, being Ravn, "The roof leaks over that bed."
One word on a stick

A Dane steps down onto the dam at Dorestad, lays a stick of ash on your thwart without a word, and walks back to his ship. There is one word cut on it, deep, in the old way, with the gate and the bar.
Nithing. You do not need it turned into Frisian. It is what you call the man who did what we did. I say we. I sat in the boat and held the rope.
The stone is up. A crew from Ripa hauled it for him. They say he stood by the open mound for a day first, and then had it closed, and asked for nothing to be put back. I sleep ashore from tonight.

I carried his first stick to you and I have carried his last. I will not carry your cloth. Nor will my brother, nor his wife's kin at the Slie. It is a long coast, Frisian. You will find it has got longer.
Burn the stick and wear the ring
Carry the ring to Saint Martin's altar at Traiectum
Send the ring back to Salhaugar with a man's price in silver (300 d)

The stick burns like any other ash. The ring sits on your arm above the elbow, a row of small horns round it, heavy and very fine. Your sons will have it after you and will be told some other story about it. In the Danish ports men look at your boat and then at the sea beside it. Ravn comes aboard at dawn each day, does his work, and goes ashore at dusk.

The priest at Saint Martin's takes the ring in both hands and asks no question a merchant cannot answer. It will hang by the altar with the other gifts, and the bishop's men will know your boat for the church's friend. "Their god will not send him anything for it," Ravn says of the old man. He is right. On the Slie and at Ripa nothing is changed.

The ring goes north in a sealed bag with three hundred pennies' weight of silver, by the same Dane, who looks at the bag a long time before he takes it. At the next moon a stick comes back. Ravn reads it. "It says: put back. That is all. He has not thanked you and he has not cursed you." He turns it over. "The other side is blank. With him that is as good as a blessing." He brings his sea-chest back aboard that night.
At Salhaugar by Hleidr a stone has been set up for Gunnvald, Hroald's son, who had the thul's seat. A Frisian crew hauled it. The old man who kept the hall's words has not named another to the seat.

The dam at Dorestad on a bright afternoon: a weathered Danish skipper in a hide cloak holds out a squared ash stick cut with runes to the merchant in his small boat, while Ravn, lean and grey-haired, watches from the bow with narrowed eyes.

The muddy river landing at Ripa under a low grey sky: a broad carter in a wool cap leans on an empty cart behind two red oxen, looking sideways at the stick in the merchant's belt; hides and whetstones stacked behind.

Open sea in thin morning fog: a Norse ship with a striped sail passes close under the small boat's lee, her master standing on the stern with one hand on the stay and a stick raised in the other, his mouth open in a shout.

A flat ferry in the middle of the Slie at evening, oars shipped, reed banks far off on both sides: a grizzled ferryman cuts a small heavy bag loose from under his thwart while the merchant sits facing him; still water, long light.

Night at sea under stars, one small lamp: Ravn bent over four rune sticks laid side by side on the thwart, his thumb on the cuts; the young English lookout watching from the bow, the steersman a dark shape at the oar.

The slope below the great timber hall at Hleidr on an autumn morning: a steward with a staff held across the path, and behind him a swineherd counting a sow and her litter out of a wattle pen on his fingers; smoke over the long roof.

Inside the hall at night, seen from the low bench by the door: two long fires, the king a far shape in the smoke with gold on his arm, and close up the young skald holding a great full horn out toward the viewer; faces turned along the benches.

A farm by six grass mounds at midday: an old blind man with white eyes on a bench against the house wall, face turned slightly away, one hand resting on a long grey uncut stone lying by the door; Ravn standing well back at the gate.

A moonless night at the mounds: one mound with raw unknit turf, two wooden spades stuck in the grass, a small jar of ale; three crewmen as dark shapes, Ravn standing apart with empty hands; the farm's roof and one dog's ears against the sky.

Morning at the foot of the mounds: four men with ropes and log rollers tilting a grey stone upright into its hole, two rows of runes, three interlocked horns and a four-armed wheel-cross cut on its face; the blind old man with his hand flat on the carving.

The hall in midwinter, silent and full: the blind old man standing alone between the two fires, face turned to the low bench, where Ravn has just risen to his feet beside the seated merchant; every head on the benches turned to him.

Inside the farmhouse at Salhaugar in spring light from the door: the old man speaking with shut eyes, the young Englishman writing on calfskin across his knees with a goose quill, Ravn beside him marking the words with a finger; sewn gatherings on the bench.

The dam at Dorestad at dusk: a single ash stick lying on the thwart of the small boat with one word of runes cut deep in it; a Dane's back walking away along the planks; Ravn on the dam with his sea-chest on his shoulder; a broad silver arm-ring on the merchant's arm.
